title: Lord of the Sabbath and the Sermon on the Plain
summary: Two Sabbath disputes, over grain picked in a field and a withered hand healed in a synagogue, deepen the conflict with the Pharisees. After a night of prayer Jesus chooses twelve apostles, then comes down to a level place and teaches a great crowd: blessings on the poor, the hungry, the weeping, and the hated, woes on the rich, the full, the laughing, and the praised, and a call to love enemies, show mercy as the Father does, judge no one, and build life on his words.
story:
Chapter 5 brought the first objections from the Pharisees over forgiveness, table company, and fasting. Now the question moves to the Sabbath, the most visible mark of Jewish faithfulness in the first century, and by verse 11 his opponents are discussing what they might do to him. These two scenes close the series of five controversies that Luke takes over from Mark 2:1-3:6, and each ends with a claim about who Jesus is: the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

Against that rising hostility Jesus forms a community. After a whole night of prayer he chooses twelve apostles, a number that recalls the twelve tribes of Israel and signals that he is gathering God's people anew. Then he comes down with them to a level place, where disciples and a great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem, and the Gentile coast of Tyre and Sidon press to touch him. The sermon that follows is his instruction for that community, the way of life that belongs to the kingdom he announced in Nazareth: good news to the poor becomes ‘Blessed are you who are poor’, and the year of the Lord's favor becomes a people who are merciful as their Father is merciful. It is the longest block of teaching so far in Luke, and it ends not with comfort but with a warning about a house that falls.
historical:
The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest commanded in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8-11, Deuteronomy 5:12-15), had become by the first century a defining sign of Jewish identity, noticed and sometimes mocked by Greek and Roman writers. Its seriousness had been sealed in blood: 1 Maccabees 2:29-41 tells how pious Jews under Antiochus IV let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath, until Mattathias and his friends decided they must defend themselves. Jewish teachers debated at length what counted as forbidden work. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, lists thirty-nine main categories, among them reaping, threshing, winnowing, and carrying (m. Shabbat 7:2). Picking grain by hand from a neighbor's field was itself allowed by Deuteronomy 23:25; the charge was that plucking and rubbing out the kernels on the Sabbath amounted to reaping and threshing. The Damascus Document from Qumran was stricter still: it forbids eating on the Sabbath anything not prepared beforehand or lying in the field (CD 10:22-23) and forbids lifting an animal out of a pit or cistern on the Sabbath (CD 11:13-14).

On healing, Jewish law agreed that danger to life overrides the Sabbath; the Mishnah says any doubt whether life is in danger sets the Sabbath aside (m. Yoma 8:6). The Mishnah's later rules forbid treatment for conditions that are not dangerous: a man with a toothache may not sip vinegar as medicine, though he may dip his food in vinegar as usual and be healed if it happens (m. Shabbat 14:4), and one may not set a broken bone (m. Shabbat 22:6). A withered hand was not an emergency. How much of this later law was held in Jesus' Galilee is uncertain, and the Pharisees themselves disagreed among themselves; the Gospels show a live debate, not a settled code.

The list of the Twelve also appears in Mark 3:16-19, Matthew 10:2-4, and Acts 1:13. Each list falls into three groups of four, always headed by Peter, Philip, and James son of Alphaeus, and always ending with Judas Iscariot. Luke's Judas son of James seems to stand where Mark and Matthew have Thaddaeus. Simon is called the Zealot, Luke's translation of the Aramaic that Mark and Matthew give as Kananaios, ‘the Cananaean’. The word may mean he was zealous for the Law, in the tradition of Phinehas and Mattathias, or connected with resistance to Rome. Richard Horsley (Bandits, Prophets, and Messiahs, with John Hanson, 1985) argued that the organized Zealot party of Josephus came into being only in the winter of AD 67 to 68, in the middle of the revolt, so the sense in Jesus' day is uncertain. The crowd includes people from Tyre and Sidon, Phoenician cities on the coast to the northwest, a hint of the Gentiles who will hear the message in Acts.
cultural:
An apostle (from the Greek apostolos, one sent) was an authorized messenger who represented the sender. The Jewish institution of the agent, the shaliach, may lie behind the title: the Mishnah says that a man's agent is as himself (m. Berakhot 5:5). Choosing twelve was a symbolic act any Jewish hearer would recognize, and Jesus later promises the Twelve that they will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (22:30). Night prayer on a mountain recalls Moses and Elijah on the mountain of God.

Much of the sermon draws on the economy of a village. The poor (ptōchoi) were not simply those with little but the destitute who had to beg, and in the Psalms and prophets the poor (anavim) are often the afflicted faithful who have no protector but God (Psalm 34:6, Isaiah 61:1). The Qumran community called itself ‘the congregation of the poor’ (4Q171). Social life across the Greek and Roman world ran on reciprocity: a benefit created an obligation, loans were made to those who could repay, and favors were returned in goods, honor, or loyalty. Seneca devoted a whole treatise, On Benefits, to its rules. Jesus' three questions in verses 32 to 34, ‘what credit is that to you?’, use charis, the word for the favor or thanks owed in that system, and his command to lend expecting nothing back cuts against it. Deuteronomy 15:7-11 had already commanded Israel to lend freely to the poor even as the year of release approached.

A slap on the cheek was an insult more than an injury; the Mishnah fixes a higher penalty for a backhanded slap than an ordinary one, because the humiliation was greater (m. Bava Qamma 8:6). The cloak (himation) was the outer garment that also served as a blanket, which the Law required a creditor to return by nightfall (Exodus 22:26-27), and the tunic (chitōn) the garment worn underneath; to give both left a person nearly bare. Luke's order, cloak first, pictures a robbery, where Matthew's order pictures a lawsuit. The Golden Rule was known in negative form: Tobit 4:15 says not to do to anyone what you hate, and the Babylonian Talmud tells how Hillel summarized the Torah for a would-be convert in the same negative words (b. Shabbat 31a). The image in verse 38 comes from the grain market: a generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down, shook it to settle it, and let it overflow into the buyer's lap, the fold of a long robe gathered above the belt and used as a pocket (compare Ruth 3:15). The speck and the beam was a proverb also known to the rabbis (b. Arakhin 16b). The closing parable fits the land's wadis, dry stream beds that could fill suddenly with winter rain and sweep away anything built on loose soil.
literary:
The chapter has three movements: two Sabbath controversies (1-11), the choosing of the Twelve and the gathering of the crowd (12-19), and the sermon (20-49). The two controversies are built as a pair, each set on a Sabbath, each with an objection from Pharisees, each turning on the keyword exestin, ‘it is lawful’ (verses 2, 4, 9), and each ending with Jesus' authority: a saying about the Son of Man and a healing that restores what was withered. The sermon on a level place has close counterparts in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7), though Luke's is much shorter, about thirty verses to Matthew's hundred and seven, and set on level ground after Jesus comes down from the mountain, while Matthew's is on the mountain. Most of Luke's sermon has parallels in Matthew's, largely in the same order: beatitudes, love of enemies, the Golden Rule, judging, the speck and the beam, trees and fruit, ‘Lord, Lord’, and the two builders.

Luke has four beatitudes, each matched by a woe in exact reverse: poor and rich, hungry and full, weeping and laughing, hated and praised. The blessings are addressed in the second person (‘you who are poor’), where Matthew's are mostly in the third person (‘the poor in spirit’), and Luke adds ‘now’ to the hunger and the weeping. Matthew has eight beatitudes (or nine, counting 5:11), no woes in the sermon, and wording that is sometimes more inward: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3) and “those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6). Scholars explain the relationship in different ways. On the two-source hypothesis, both evangelists drew on a common collection of sayings, often called Q, and Luke's shorter, more concrete form is usually thought closer to it. On the Farrer hypothesis, argued by Austin Farrer (1955) and Mark Goodacre (The Case Against Q, 2002), Luke knew Matthew and abbreviated and rearranged his sermon. Many harmonizers since Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.19) have held that Jesus gave similar teaching on more than one occasion, or that the level place was a plateau on the mountain.

The sermon moves from blessing and woe (20-26) to love of enemies and mercy (27-38), to judging, teachers, and fruit (39-45), and ends with a question and a parable of two builders (46-49), as Matthew's does. Its center is verse 36, “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful”, where Matthew has ‘perfect’. The section on enemies is framed by the same command, love your enemies (verses 27 and 35), and built on the contrast between the world's reciprocity (32-34) and God's kindness to the ungrateful and wicked (35).

outline.t: A withered hand healed on the Sabbath
A night of prayer and the choosing of the Twelve
Crowds gather on a level place
Love your enemies; be merciful as your Father
Blind guides, specks and beams, trees and fruit

doctrines.note: Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he keeps it in the synagogue and claims to be its Lord (verse 5). He defends his disciples from Scripture and reframes the question from what may be done to what ought to be done: to do good and to save life (verse 9). The Sabbath's purpose, rest and release given by God (Deuteronomy 5:15), is honored by healing on it. How the Sabbath applies to Christians is debated among the churches.

Jesus forms a people around himself, choosing twelve from a wider circle of disciples after a night of prayer and naming them apostles, those sent. The number recalls Israel's twelve tribes, and the sermon describes the common life of that renewed people, marked by mercy, generosity, and refusal to judge.

The kingdom of God belongs to the poor (verse 20) and brings a great reversal: the hungry filled, the weeping laughing, the comfortable emptied. The kingdom is present (yours is the kingdom) and future (you will be filled). Its ethic reflects its King, who is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.

Luke's woes address the rich and the well fed directly: they have already received their comfort, paid in full (verse 24). The sermon commands giving to everyone who asks and lending without expecting return, and warns that possessions can become the only consolation a person will ever have. Luke's Gospel develops the theme in 12:13-21, 16:19-31, and 18:18-30.

The center of the sermon is love for enemies, expressed in four actions: love, do good, bless, pray (verses 27-28). It goes beyond the reciprocity that even sinners practice and is grounded in the character of God, who is kind to the ungrateful and wicked, so that those who love this way show themselves children of the Most High.

words.note: Exesti, it is lawful, it is permitted. It occurs about thirty times in the New Testament and is the keyword of both Sabbath scenes: the Pharisees ask why the disciples do what is not lawful (verse 2), Jesus answers that David ate what was lawful only for priests (verse 4), and then asks whether it is lawful to do good or to do evil (verse 9). The word frames the question as legal permission; Jesus' final question turns it into moral obligation.

Apostolos, one sent, a messenger, an apostle. It occurs about eighty times in the New Testament, six in Luke's Gospel and twenty-eight in Acts, far more than in Matthew (once) or Mark (once or twice). It comes from apostellō, to send, the verb of Jesus' own sending in 4:18 and 4:43. In verse 13 Jesus himself gives the twelve the name, and in Luke-Acts ‘the apostles’ usually means the Twelve, witnesses of Jesus from John's baptism to the resurrection (Acts 1:21-22).

Makarios, blessed, fortunate, happy. It occurs about fifty times in the New Testament, fifteen in Luke. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew ashrei, as in “Blessed is the man” of Psalm 1:1, a declaration of someone's true standing before God rather than a wish or a feeling. BDAG glosses it as privileged recipient of divine favor. Jesus pronounces the poor and grieving blessed not because their suffering is good but because the kingdom is theirs and God will reverse their condition.

Ptōchos, poor, destitute, a beggar. It occurs about thirty-four times in the New Testament, ten in Luke, more than any other book. Greek distinguished the ptōchos, who had to beg, from the penēs, the working poor who had little. In the Septuagint ptōchos renders the Hebrew words for the afflicted and oppressed poor (Isaiah 61:1), who look to God. Luke joins the economic sense, clear in Lazarus at the rich man's gate (16:20), with that biblical sense of dependence.

Ouai, woe, alas. It occurs about forty-six times in the New Testament, fifteen in Luke, and in the Septuagint renders the Hebrew hoy, the prophets' cry of lament and warning over those on the road to ruin (Isaiah 5:8-22, Amos 6:1). The woes are not curses so much as grief-stricken warnings over people whose comfort has already been paid out in full. First Enoch 94 to 99 contains similar woes on those who trust in their riches.

Oiktirmōn, compassionate, merciful. It occurs only three times in the New Testament, twice in verse 36 and once in James 5:11, where the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. In the Septuagint it belongs to God's self-description to Moses (Exodus 34:6, oiktirmōn kai eleēmōn), and it describes God in the Psalms (103:8, 145:8). Matthew's parallel says be perfect as your Father is perfect; Luke's wording puts mercy at the center of what it means to resemble God.

Apelpizō. It occurs only here in the New Testament. In ordinary Greek it means to despair or give up hope, but in verse 35 the context requires ‘expecting nothing back’, taking apo- as ‘back’ with elpizō, to hope. A few manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus, read mēdena, ‘despairing of no one’. The Latin Vulgate's nihil inde sperantes, ‘hoping for nothing from it’, made the verse a medieval proof text against charging interest on loans.

Echthros, enemy, hostile. It occurs about thirty-two times in the New Testament and covers personal, religious, and national enemies alike. In Luke Zechariah's song had praised God for salvation from our enemies (1:71, 1:74); now Jesus commands his disciples to love them (verses 27 and 35). In a land under Roman rule, with villages divided by feuds and neighbors who could be informers, the command was startling. Paul echoes it (Romans 12:14-21).

christ:
Jesus claims to be Lord of the Sabbath, a day God himself instituted at creation (Genesis 2:2-3) and gave to Israel as a sign (Exodus 31:13). He reads the story of David eating the holy bread as a precedent for his own followers, which implies that one greater than David is present, and when the Pharisees watch to accuse him he makes the healing public and asks the question they cannot answer. The restoration of the withered hand shows what the Sabbath rest is for, and Luke later adds two more Sabbath healings (13:10-17, 14:1-6), in one of which Jesus says a daughter of Abraham ought to be released from her bond on the Sabbath day.

He spends a whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve, one of many turning points in Luke marked by his prayer (3:21, 5:16, 9:18, 9:28-29, 22:41-44). The crowds press to touch him because power goes out from him to heal them all. In the sermon he speaks with his own authority and pronounces God's blessings and woes, a prophet's office and more. He blesses those who are hated ‘because of the Son of Man’, linking discipleship to loyalty to his person, and he makes the house that stands depend on hearing and doing his words, the place Israel's Scriptures give to the words of the LORD (Isaiah 28:16-17, Proverbs 10:25). The question “Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but not do what I say?” assumes that he is rightly called Lord.

The ethic he teaches is the life he lives. He blesses the poor and becomes poor; he tells his followers to offer the other cheek and lets himself be struck and mocked (22:63-64), fulfilling the servant's words, “I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard” (Isaiah 50:6). He tells them to pray for those who mistreat them, and on the cross he prays, according to most manuscripts, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (23:34). The merciful Father of verse 36 is the father of the prodigal son in chapter 15, and the Son who teaches this mercy is the one through whom the Father shows it.
interpretation:
The sermon's sayings were among the first words of Jesus the church quoted. The Didache (1:3-5) repeats the commands to bless those who curse, pray for enemies, and give to everyone who asks; 1 Clement 13:2, around AD 96, cites the Lord's words to be merciful, forgive, and measure as one would be measured; and Polycarp (To the Philippians 2:3) quotes them again. Justin Martyr (First Apology 15-16, around 155) set the love of enemies before the emperor as proof of what Christians are taught. Ambrose of Milan (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke, book 5) read Luke's four beatitudes as the four cardinal virtues, temperance, justice, prudence, and fortitude, and argued that Luke's four contain Matthew's eight. Jerome (Letter 52.8) recorded asking Gregory of Nazianzus the meaning of the puzzling ‘second-first Sabbath’ in verse 1, and Gregory joked that he would explain it in church, where the applause would force Jerome to claim he understood.

The commands on enemies have divided Christians more than almost any other text. Augustine (Letter 138, to Marcellinus, 412) answered pagan critics who said such teaching made Christians useless citizens: the command to turn the other cheek requires an inward disposition, readiness to pardon rather than to take revenge, not a rule for how a state must defend a province. Medieval theology distinguished precepts binding on all from counsels of perfection for those under vows. Martin Luther (On Temporal Authority, 1523) held that Christians must suffer wrong for themselves but may bear the sword as rulers and soldiers to protect their neighbors, while the Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527) declared that the sword is ordained by God outside the perfection of Christ and is not for his followers. Leo Tolstoy (The Kingdom of God Is Within You, 1894) read ‘resist not evil’ as an absolute command against all force, and Gandhi credited the book with shaping his commitment to nonviolence. Dietrich Bonhoeffer (Discipleship, 1937) insisted the commands mean what they say for those who follow Christ, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s sermon Loving Your Enemies (in Strength to Love, 1963) made them the root of the civil rights movement's discipline. Reinhold Niebuhr argued that the ethic is an impossible ideal that judges every political order but cannot govern one, and John Howard Yoder (The Politics of Jesus, 1972) that it is a real social ethic for the church. Walter Wink (Engaging the Powers, 1992) read the cheek and cloak sayings as a third way between violence and passivity.

The verse on lending (35) shaped the medieval prohibition of usury, and Luke's blessing of the poor became central to liberation theology, as in Gustavo Gutiérrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971), and to Catholic social teaching's language of a preferential option for the poor. The Sabbath scenes have been read in debates over the Christian day of rest. Ignatius of Antioch (To the Magnesians 9) described Christians as no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's day; the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21) holds that the Sabbath command continues as the Christian Sabbath on the first day; Luther's Large Catechism (1529) treats the third commandment as a day for hearing God's word, not a binding law of rest; and Seventh-day Adventists keep the seventh day. Samuele Bacchiocchi (From Sabbath to Sunday, 1977) and D. A. Carson's volume From Sabbath to Lord's Day (1982) set out rival accounts. Hans Dieter Betz's Hermeneia commentary (The Sermon on the Mount, 1995) treats the Sermon on the Plain alongside Matthew's. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C reads 6:17-26, 6:27-38, and 6:39-49 on the sixth to eighth Sundays after the Epiphany, and 6:20-31 on All Saints' Day.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from the manuscripts. In verse 1 the King James Version reads ‘on the second sabbath after the first’, translating deuteroprōtos, ‘second-first’, found in Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, and the Byzantine text. The word occurs nowhere else in Greek literature, and the earliest manuscripts, including Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus, lack it. Suggested meanings include the first Sabbath after the second day of Passover, when the count of weeks to Pentecost began (Leviticus 23:10-16); Bruce Metzger's Textual Commentary suggests instead that it arose from copyists' marginal notes counting the Sabbaths in these chapters. Since the omission has the earlier support and the word is so hard to explain as original, modern editions omit it.

Codex Bezae, a Greek and Latin manuscript copied around AD 400, moves verse 5 to follow verse 10 and puts in its place a saying found in no other manuscript. On the same day, it reports, Jesus saw a man working on the Sabbath and told him that if he knew what he was doing he was blessed, but if he did not know, he was cursed and a transgressor of the law. Some have wondered whether it preserves an old independent tradition; Jason Robert Combs (Journal for the Study of the New Testament 42, 2019) argued that it arose in later Christian polemic over Sabbath observance. No modern translation includes it.

In verse 35 most manuscripts read mēden apelpizontes, ‘expecting nothing back’, but Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Washingtonianus, and the Sinaitic Syriac read mēdena, ‘despairing of no one’, probably an accidental repetition of a letter. In verse 48 the Byzantine text and the King James Version read ‘for it was founded upon a rock’, taken from Matthew 7:25, where the earliest manuscripts read ‘because it was well built’. In verse 10 later manuscripts and the King James Version add ‘whole as the other’ from Matthew 12:13. Verse 29's ‘one cheek’ lacks Matthew's ‘right’ in every manuscript, a detail that matters to interpretations built on a backhanded blow.

teach.big: The Lord of the Sabbath gathers a new people and teaches them to live by the reversals of God's kingdom, loving enemies and showing mercy as the Father does, and to build their lives on hearing and doing his words.

outline.t: Scripture itself shows that human need can take precedence over holy regulations, and the Son of Man has authority over the Sabbath.
Refusing to do good when one can is itself doing harm; Jesus restores the man publicly while his critics harden in rage.
Jesus prays through the night before choosing his apostles, an ordinary and flawed group that includes a tax collector, a zealot, and a traitor.
Jesus comes down to the crowd, Jew and Gentile, and power goes out from him to heal them all.
God's verdict reverses the world's: the poor, hungry, grieving, and rejected who belong to Jesus are blessed, and the comfortable and praised are warned.
Disciples love enemies with concrete actions, refuse retaliation, give without calculation, and show the mercy their Father shows the ungrateful.
Before correcting others, disciples examine themselves, choose their teachers well, and let a changed heart produce good fruit.
Calling Jesus Lord means doing what he says; only a life built on his words survives the flood.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first uses the Sabbath scenes to picture the Pharisees as heartless legalists and Judaism as a religion of rules. The Pharisees were debating a real question about honoring God's command, the Mishnah itself sets aside the Sabbath to save life, and Luke says only some Pharisees objected. The point is Jesus' authority and the Sabbath's purpose, not a caricature. A second makes the beatitudes into a spiritual ladder of attitudes to attain; Luke's are God's declarations over people in real poverty, hunger, and grief who belong to Jesus. A third spiritualizes the poor so completely that the woes to the rich lose their force, or, in the opposite direction, treats poverty as holy in itself and forgets that the blessing is spoken to disciples.

With the commands on enemies, avoid two errors. One reduces them to impossible ideals that no one is really expected to keep, which empties them; the other applies them mechanically in ways Jesus did not intend, for instance telling victims of abuse that turning the other cheek means staying in danger. Jesus himself protested an unjust blow (John 18:22-23). Verse 37 does not forbid all moral judgment, since verses 43 to 45 require discerning fruit; it forbids condemning others while excusing oneself. Verse 38 is often used to promise financial return for giving to a ministry. It concerns the measure of mercy and generosity God returns, and the context is lending to enemies without expecting repayment.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses hard on several kinds of people. Those who have been abused or are in danger need to hear that loving an enemy does not require remaining under violence or pretending that harm was not harm; forgiveness and refusal of revenge are not the same as returning to an abuser, and safety and justice are not revenge. Those who are poor or grieving should hear the blessings as God's word to them, not as a reason others may ignore their need. The scrupulous may read ‘do not judge’ and ‘first take the beam out’ as a demand for endless self-examination; Jesus' goal is clear sight to help a brother, not paralysis. And those who have been judged harshly by a church may find in Jesus' defense of his disciples and his healing on the Sabbath a Lord who puts people before the scruples of the watchers.

hard.q: Did Jesus break the Sabbath, and are these scenes fair to the Pharisees?
hard.a:
The objection comes from historians and from Jewish readers. E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) judged the setting of the grainfield scene extraordinarily unrealistic, since Pharisees did not organize themselves into groups to spend their Sabbaths in Galilean fields waiting to catch someone transgressing, and concluded that such stories do not describe actual debates between Jesus and others; in his later Jewish Law from Jesus to the Mishnah (1990) he argued that the Sabbath disputes reported of Jesus fall within the range of ordinary Jewish legal debate. Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes (The Religion of Jesus the Jew, 1993) read Jesus as an observant Jew whose disputes about the Law were arguments within Judaism. On this view the Gospels, written after Jewish and Christian communities had divided, sharpened the conflict and made the Pharisees villains, with lasting harm to Jewish-Christian relations. Rabbinic tradition even preserves a saying close to Mark 2:27: Rabbi Simeon ben Menasya taught that the Sabbath is given to you, and you are not given to the Sabbath (Mekhilta on Exodus 31:14).

Others answer that the scenes fit what is known of first-century debate. Maurice Casey (Aramaic Sources of Mark's Gospel, 1998) argued that the grainfield incident is historically plausible and concerns the poor's right to glean at the edges of fields, a question Pharisees did discuss, and the Qumran Damascus Document shows how strict some Jews were about food and animals on the Sabbath. Many Christian scholars, including contributors to From Sabbath to Lord's Day (edited by D. A. Carson, 1982), grant that Jesus kept the Sabbath and did not break the written Law, and locate the offense chiefly in his claim to authority over it: the argument ends not with a ruling but with ‘the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath’. Luke's own portrait is not uniformly hostile: some Pharisees dine with Jesus and warn him (7:36, 13:31), and Gamaliel defends the apostles (Acts 5:34-39). Whether Jesus' actions broke the Pharisees' interpretation or only provoked debate, and how much the evangelists shaped these stories, remain open questions. Christians also still disagree about how the Sabbath command applies to them, from Seventh-day Sabbath keeping to a Christian Sabbath on Sunday to a freedom in which every day belongs to the Lord.

hard.q: Did Jesus mean these commands literally: turn the other cheek, give to everyone who asks, never demand your goods back?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the objection comes from two directions. Critics of Christianity, from the pagan Volusianus in Augustine's day to modern political realists, argue that an ethic of non-resistance is either unlivable or irresponsible: no society can protect the weak if it refuses force, and no household survives if it gives to everyone who asks. Reinhold Niebuhr concluded that the ethic is an impossible ideal that judges every human order but cannot direct one. From the other side, Leo Tolstoy (The Kingdom of God Is Within You, 1894) and the Anabaptist tradition from the Schleitheim Confession (1527) to John Howard Yoder (1972) argue that Christians have evaded Jesus' plain words for centuries, and that these commands are meant to be obeyed by his followers, including refusing violence even in self-defense or war.

The main Christian responses differ, and none has won. The tradition from Augustine (Letter 138) and Luther (On Temporal Authority, 1523) holds that the commands govern a disciple's personal response to wrong and forbid revenge, but do not forbid the proper use of force by governments to protect the weak, which Paul describes in Romans 13:1-7. The peace-church tradition holds that the church is called to embody the kingdom's way now, whatever the cost. Walter Wink (Engaging the Powers, 1992) read the sayings as a creative third way that refuses both passivity and violence. Many readers note that Jesus speaks in vivid, even hyperbolic images to overturn instinct, and that when an officer struck him before Annas he protested the blow rather than offering the other cheek (John 18:22-23). On poverty and possessions, some read Luke's blessings as God's special concern for the economically poor, and others as describing the pious poor who depend on God, close to Matthew's poor in spirit; Luke's text suggests both, since the blessing is spoken to disciples who have left everything. Whatever the application, the commands are not less than a refusal of revenge and a generosity that resembles the Father's, and Christians who disagree on war and self-defense agree that they condemn hatred.

observe: What do the Pharisees object to in each Sabbath scene, and how does Jesus answer each time?
Compare the four blessings (verses 20-23) with the four woes (verses 24-26). How does each woe mirror a blessing?
What four actions does Jesus command toward enemies in verses 27-28, and what reason does he give in verse 35?
interpret: What does it mean that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, and why does Jesus frame the question as doing good or doing harm?
Why might Luke's beatitudes be addressed to ‘you’ and include ‘now’, and how do they differ from Matthew's?
How does verse 36, be merciful as your Father is merciful, summarize the sermon, and how does it relate to verse 37's command not to judge?
apply: Which of the four woes speaks most directly to your own situation, and what would it mean to take it seriously?
Name one person who has wronged you. What would it look like, concretely, to do good to them, bless them, and pray for them, without pretending the wrong did not happen?
The two builders both heard Jesus' words; only one acted on them. What is one word of Jesus you know well but have not built on?
